paragraphs: Ireland wants to cut €141 billion from the next long-term budget of the European Union. This budget will pay for EU plans from 2028 to 2034. The first plan from the European Commission says the budget should be about €1.7 trillion.

Ireland has an important job in the talks. Until the end of this year, it leads the meetings of EU countries. For months, Irish officials spoke quietly with every country and with the EU offices. On Saturday, the Government showed its plan, which is called a "negotiating box".

In the Irish plan, money for farmers and for poorer regions does not get smaller. Instead, the EU would spend less on help for poor countries, on the costs of running its offices and on a new fund to help business.

Many people did not like the plan. Some rich countries, such as Germany, the Netherlands and the Nordic countries, want a much smaller budget. They want to cut several hundred billion euro. A Swedish minister said the plan still costs too much. But another big group, with Italy, Spain and Poland, says it will fight any cuts to money for farms and regions. A leader in the European Parliament also said no to the plan. He said it gives too little money to defence, farmers and regions.
Thomas Byrne, the Irish minister for Europe, said the plan protects the old and important EU policies as much as the countries wanted.

All 27 countries and the European Parliament must say yes to the budget. Leaders want a deal before the end of 2026, partly because France will choose a new president next spring. Irish officials said quietly that if every side is unhappy, the plan has done its job.

Ireland has proposed cutting €141 billion from the European Union's next long-term budget, which will cover the years 2028 to 2034. The draft budget prepared by the European Commission currently stands at about €1.7 trillion.

Ireland is playing a central role in the talks because it holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU until the end of the year. After months of quiet diplomacy with national capitals and EU institutions, the Government published its compromise plan, known as a "negotiating box", on Saturday.

Under the Irish plan, farm subsidies and "cohesion" funding for poorer regions would be protected from further cuts. Instead, savings would come from development aid, the running costs of EU institutions and a planned fund to boost competitiveness.

The proposal quickly drew criticism from several sides. A group of so-called "frugal" countries, led by Germany and including the Netherlands and Nordic states, wants a budget several hundred billion euro smaller. Sweden's European affairs minister said the figures still meant an increase that was not affordable. Meanwhile, a large group including Italy, Spain and Poland has promised to resist any cuts to farming or regional money. A senior member of the European Parliament also rejected the plan, saying it would underfund defence, farmers and regions.
Minister of State for European Affairs Thomas Byrne said the plan protected the union's traditional policies as far as member states wanted.

All 27 member states and the European Parliament must approve the budget. Leaders hope to reach a deal before the end of 2026, partly because a French presidential election is due next spring. Irish diplomats said privately that if every side is unhappy, the plan has done its job.

Ireland has tabled a proposal to trim €141 billion from the European Union's forthcoming seven-year budget, which will run from 2028 to 2034. The European Commission's draft currently amounts to roughly €1.7 trillion.

Ireland finds itself at the heart of the negotiations, as it holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU until the year's end. Following months of discreet diplomacy with national capitals and EU institutions, the Government unveiled its compromise blueprint, dubbed a "negotiating box", on Saturday.

The Irish blueprint shields agricultural subsidies and "cohesion" funding for less prosperous regions from further reductions. Savings would instead be found in development aid, the administrative overheads of EU institutions and a proposed fund intended to bolster competitiveness.

The proposal swiftly came under fire from several quarters. A bloc of so-called "frugal" nations, spearheaded by Germany and comprising the Netherlands and the Nordic states, is holding out for a budget several hundred billion euro leaner. Sweden's European affairs minister contended that the figures still implied an unaffordable rise. Meanwhile, a sizeable coalition including Italy, Spain and Poland has vowed to fiercely resist any erosion of farming or regional funds. A senior member of the European Parliament likewise dismissed the plan, arguing that it would shortchange defence, farmers and regions.
Minister of State for European Affairs Thomas Byrne maintained that the plan had safeguarded the union's traditional policies to the extent that member states desired.

The budget requires the unanimous backing of all 27 member states as well as the consent of the European Parliament. Leaders aim to strike a deal before the close of 2026, partly because a French presidential election looms next spring. Irish diplomats conceded privately that if every camp is dissatisfied, the plan has fulfilled its purpose.

Ireland has put forward a proposal to reduce the European Union's forthcoming multiannual budget, covering the period from 2028 to 2034, by €141 billion. The draft prepared by the European Commission currently amounts to approximately €1.7 trillion.

Ireland occupies a pivotal position in the negotiations, since it holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU until the end of the year. Following several months of discreet consultation with national governments and EU institutions, the Government published its compromise framework, referred to as a "negotiating box", on Saturday.

Under this framework, agricultural subsidies and "cohesion" funding for less developed regions would be protected from further reductions. Consequently, savings would be derived from development aid, the administrative expenditure of EU institutions and a proposed fund designed to enhance competitiveness.

The proposal has nevertheless attracted substantial criticism from several directions. A group of so-called "frugal" states, led by Germany and comprising the Netherlands and the Nordic countries, is advocating a budget that is several hundred billion euro smaller. Sweden's European affairs minister asserted that the figures still represented an unsustainable increase. Conversely, a considerable alliance including Italy, Spain and Poland has pledged to oppose any reduction in agricultural or regional allocations. A senior member of the European Parliament similarly rejected the framework, maintaining that it would provide insufficient resources for defence, farmers and regions.
Minister of State for European Affairs Thomas Byrne stated that the framework had preserved the union's traditional policies to the degree that member states had requested.

Final approval is contingent upon the unanimous agreement of all 27 member states and the consent of the European Parliament. Leaders intend to conclude an agreement before the end of 2026, partly because a French presidential election is scheduled for next spring. Irish diplomats acknowledged privately that if every party remains dissatisfied, the framework has achieved its objective.
